clue.text: Way out in front, was ahead!

definitions.note: in cricket, being bowled is one way a batsman can be out

parts.note: the bow is the front end of a ship
to have led is to have been ahead, out in front

explanation.surface: An exclamation about someone who was far out in front and leading the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way out in front' reads as one phrase meaning well ahead, but it splits: 'Way out' is the definition and 'front' gives BOW. BOWLED is a cricket dismissal: the ball hits the batsman's wicket.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket batsmen can be dismissed several ways, and being bowled is one of those ways of getting out.

clue.text: Flour, say, for bread

definitions.meaning: flour sounds like flower, and a flower is something that blooms, so this is a thing in bloom
a large crusty loaf with diagonal slashes across its top

explanation.surface: Flour given as an example of what goes into a loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition plays on 'flour' sounding like 'flower', one that blooms. A BLOOMER is also a common British loaf with a slashed top.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant in flower can be called a bloomer, and in British bakeries a bloomer is a type of crusty white loaf.

clue.text: Rubbish sci-fi film watched after promotion

indicators.note: in a down clue, promotion moves the letters upwards, so the whole sequence is read from bottom to top

parts.note: E.T. is Spielberg's science-fiction film about an alien
saw means watched

explanation.surface: A dreadful science-fiction film was seen after it had been heavily promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after promotion' turns the joined letters ETSAW upward in this down entry, reading them backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Waste and rubbish are synonyms for discarded, worthless material.

clue.text: Final moves by English celebrity to impress BBC chief

indicators.note: to impress is to press a mark into something, so one piece is pushed inside the other

parts.note: a big name is a celebrity
the head of the BBC is the Director-General, DG

explanation.surface: A celebrity's last moves made to win over the head of the BBC.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to impress' signals one piece pressed into another. The BBC's head is its Director-General, a convention solvers may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the endgame is the last phase of play, when the final moves are made.

clue.text: Last of plant matter, organic material

indicators.note: asks for the final letter of the word plant

parts.note: an issue is a matter under discussion

explanation.surface: The remains of a plant, matter that counts as organic material.
explanation.definitionFit: Tissue is the cellular material that makes up living organisms, so it is organic matter.

clue.text: Popular? Well I never did! (Clinton)

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
hale means healthy, well

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at someone's popularity.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Clinton famously said he had smoked marijuana but 'didn't inhale', so the parenthesis makes the bracketed phrase his line. 'Well I never did!' reads as a stock exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Clinton claimed he tried cannabis without drawing the smoke into his lungs, the act he 'never did'.

clue.text: A ninja, might you say, in Chinese republic

indicators.note: the phrase must be spoken, here in a mock Chinese accent, to sound like the answer

parts.note: a ninja is a Japanese warrior but not one of the samurai class, so you might call one 'samurai? no'

explanation.surface: Wondering what a ninja would be called in Chinese.
explanation.walkthrough: A ninja is a 'samurai? no', and said aloud in a jokey accent that sounds like SAN MARINO. 'Chinese' is part of the sound signal, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: San Marino is a tiny independent republic surrounded by Italy, one of the oldest republics in the world.

clue.text: Horse docked before bovine about 22 September?

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: equine means a horse
an ox is a bovine animal

explanation.surface: A horse with a cropped tail placed in front of a cow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' cuts the final E from EQUINE, leaving EQUIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The autumn equinox, when day and night are of equal length, falls around 22 or 23 September.

clue.text: Green council's a real nightmare

indicators.note: a nightmare is a chaotic mess, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the word council's, with its S kept as a letter

explanation.surface: A complaint that the local council is a real nightmare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nightmare' rearranges COUNCILSAREAL. Caroline Lucas was leader of the Green Party of England and Wales and its first MP, for Brighton Pavilion.
explanation.definitionFit: She was the leading figure of Britain's Green Party, so 'Green' names her by political allegiance.

clue.text: Manager, a stud

definitions.meaning: the person in charge at work, the head
a raised knob or ornamental stud, as on a shield

explanation.surface: A manager who fancies himself something of a stud.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is someone in charge of workers, and a boss is also a round raised knob or stud.

clue.text: Fuzzy aphid requiring a sense that's clear

indicators.note: fuzzy means blurred and unclear, so the letters of aphid are jumbled

parts.note: nous is common sense

explanation.surface: A blurred greenfly needing a sense that is clear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuzzy' rearranges APHID into DIAPH.
explanation.definitionFit: Diaphanous fabric is so thin it is see-through, effectively transparent.

clue.text: A second president recalled as brainless life form

parts.note: mo is short for a moment, a second

indicators.note: called back, so the president's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln, US president

explanation.surface: A second-rate president is remembered as a brainless creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns ABE into EBA.
explanation.definitionFit: This single-celled organism has no nervous system at all, so it is literally without a brain.

clue.text: Artist's medium, or impressively large, portrait for starters isn't common

indicators.note: starters are the opening letters of the four words before

parts.note: ain't is a nonstandard, common form of isn't

explanation.surface: Describing a painting medium suited to an impressively large portrait that is out of the ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigment bound in linseed oil is a classic material that painters work with.

clue.text: Criminal hit copper — that's ominous!

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked, so these letters are twisted out of order

explanation.surface: A criminal hitting a policeman, which bodes badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' rearranges HITCOPPER. 'copper' looks like a PC or CU, but its letters are used whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Something prophetic foretells the future, and an ominous sign foretells trouble.

clue.text: American author, one trying to be a poor writer

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, American writer
a taster is one who tries food or drink

explanation.surface: A US writer who was just trying to be a bad one.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetaster is a writer of inferior, trashy verse, a bad poet.

clue.text: Flirt offering a kiss after thirty seconds?

indicators.note: after places the kiss behind the thirty seconds

parts.note: half a minute: the first half of the word minute, written in full
X is the conventional kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A flirt offering a kiss after only half a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thirty seconds' is half a minute, so the first half of MINUTE, MIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A minx is a cheeky, flirtatious young woman.

clue.text: View wimp, ultimately, as drip

parts.note: to view is to see

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of wimp

explanation.surface: Looking upon a weakling as a drip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drip' looks like another word for the wimp, but here it is a verb meaning to leak slowly.
explanation.definitionFit: To seep and to drip are both to ooze out slowly, a little at a time.

clue.text: Nonsense of USA and Iran, prehistoric

indicators.note: nonsense is garbled talk, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: The nonsense between America and Iran is positively prehistoric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nonsense of' rearranges USAIRAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Saurian means lizard-like, as dinosaurs were, so it suits creatures of the distant past.

clue.text: Reporter putting five points to the nation

parts.note: north, east, west, south and west again, five compass points
Oman is a nation in Arabia

explanation.surface: A journalist making five points to the country.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who reports news for a paper or broadcaster is a female journalist.

clue.text: South African application that may be panned?

parts.note: SA stands for South Africa or South African
usage means application, use

explanation.surface: A South African app that might get savaged by critics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'panned' suggests harsh reviews, but a banger is fried in a pan. 'application' suggests a phone app.
explanation.definitionFit: Sausages are typically cooked in a frying pan, so one is a thing that gets panned.

clue.text: Publication priest set up that's mercurial?

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting up lifts the letters so they read upward

parts.note: mag is short for magazine, a publication
a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist priest

explanation.surface: A magazine a priest put together that is fickle in tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' reverses MAGLAMA in this down entry. 'mercurial' suggests moody, but means containing mercury.
explanation.definitionFit: An amalgam is an alloy of mercury with another metal, as in dental fillings.

clue.text: Rare shock, leader in competition getting held

indicators.note: the letter is getting held within the other word, contained inside it

parts.note: a scare is a fright or shock

indicators.note: the leader is the opening letter of the word competition

explanation.surface: An unusual shock when the competition leader is arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting held' puts C inside SCARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scarce is in short supply, seldom found.

clue.text: Half as much fun twirling moustache?

indicators.note: twirling spins the letters round into a new order
takes the first half of the two-letter word as

explanation.surface: Twirling a moustache is only half as much fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' gives A from AS, and 'twirling' rearranges AMUCHFUN. Fu Manchu is the fictional villain whose long drooping moustache is named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, thin, downward-hanging moustache is named after the fictional villain Dr Fu Manchu.

clue.text: Far from bloody outstanding article — deservedly so?

definitions.text: Far from bloody outstanding article — deservedly so?

indicators.note: read as out-standing, the first piece stands outside the second

parts.note: un-red, not red, so far from bloody
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece that is nowhere near brilliant, and rightly nobody reads it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding' looks like praise but means standing outside: UNRED around A. 'bloody' is the British intensifier, like 'damned'.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes a mediocre article that nobody gets through, which is fittingly left unopened by readers.

clue.text: Slam meat in the oven?

definitions.meaning: to slam is to criticise harshly
a joint of meat cooking in the oven

explanation.surface: Criticising the joint cooking in the oven.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast someone is to criticise them severely, and a roast is a joint cooked in the oven.

clue.text: Antique objects found in battered raincoat after the last King George

indicators.note: after places the rearranged coat behind the royal numeral

parts.note: George VI was the last British king named George, giving VI

indicators.note: battered means knocked about, so the letters of raincoat are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Old curios turning up in a worn-out mac once owned by George VI.
explanation.walkthrough: 'battered' rearranges RAINCOAT into CTORIANA.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoriana are collectable objects dating from the reign of Queen Victoria.

clue.text: Freight's seagoing, by the sound of it, for legendary ship

indicators.text: seagoing, by the sound of it
indicators.note: sea is said like the letter C, so sea going means that letter departs

parts.note: cargo is freight

explanation.surface: A ship of legend carrying ocean-going freight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seagoing' looks like a description of a ship, but splits as 'sea going': the letter C, which sounds like sea, goes from CARGO.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argo was the ship in Greek myth on which Jason and the Argonauts sailed.

clue.text: Anxiety shown by figure returning to collect mother, finally

indicators.note: collecting takes something in, so the letter is gathered inside
returning means the number is read backwards

parts.note: seven is a number, a figure

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of mother

explanation.surface: Nerves shown by someone heading back to pick up their mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns SEVEN into NEVES, and 'to collect' puts R inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerves is a plural word for nervousness, a state of worry or anxiety.

clue.text: Dividing wall takes a month? I'm not sure

parts.note: Sept is short for September
um is a hesitant sound of uncertainty

explanation.surface: Building a partition takes a month, or does it?
explanation.definitionFit: In anatomy a septum is a partition between two cavities, as in the nose.
